facts.statement: Marasuchus is an early genus of dinosauriform archosaur and a close relative of dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Marasuchus (meaning "Mara crocodile") is an early genus of dinosauriform archosaur, one of the closest relatives of dinosaurs.

facts.statement: The species Marasuchus lilloensis was originally named Lagosuchus lilloensis in 1972.
facts.quote: Marasuchus lilloensis was originally designated as Lagosuchus lilloensis in 1972.

facts.statement: Marasuchus fossils were named after specimens stored at the PVL museum in San Miguel de Tucuman.
facts.quote: It was named for a few well-preserved dinosauriform fossils stored at PVL, a museum in San Miguel de Tucuman.

facts.statement: The first known remains of Marasuchus were found during a 1964-1965 paleontological expedition.
facts.quote: Many Chanares fossils, including the first known remains of Marasuchus, were unearthed as a result of a 1964-1965 paleontological expedition.

facts.statement: Alfred Romer described the fossils found during the expedition in a series of papers.
facts.quote: Discoveries made during the expedition were later described in a series of papers by Alfred Romer from the MCZ.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen PVL 3871 was collected by Jose Bonaparte in 1969.
facts.quote: The holotype, PVL 3871, was collected by Bonaparte in 1969.

facts.statement: Marasuchus lived in the Late Triassic (early Carnian stage) in what is now La Rioja Province, Argentina.
facts.quote: Both names have been applied to small bipedal dinosauriform fossils from the same time and place: the Late Triassic (early Carnian stage) of what is now La Rioja Province, Argentina.

facts.statement: Marasuchus fossils come from the Chañares Formation, dated to 235 to 234 million years ago.
facts.quote: Marasuchus hails from the Chañares Formation of Argentina. This formation has been dated to the early Carnian (the first stage of the Late Triassic), about 235 to 234 million years old.

facts.statement: Marasuchus was roughly the size of a pigeon with a curved neck, long tail, and meat-eating teeth.
facts.quote: Marasuchus was roughly the size of a pigeon, with an curved neck, long tail, and teeth consistent with a diet of mostly meat.

facts.statement: Its body proportions suggest Marasuchus was probably bipedal, walking on its hindlimbs.
facts.quote: For example, its proportions indicate that it was probably bipedal (walking on only its hindlimbs), like early dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Marasuchus had long, slender limbs where the hindlimbs were about twice the length of the forelimbs.
facts.quote: The limbs were long and slender, with the hindlimbs about twice the length of the forelimbs.

facts.statement: Marasuchus had a relatively long neck with an S-shaped curve and a very long, thin tail that was deeper at the base.
facts.quote: The neck was relatively long for an archosaur, with an S-shaped curve as its default position, while the tail was very long and thin, though deeper at its base.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Marasuchus had a femur measuring 5.75 cm (2.26 inches), which is 40-50% larger than that of Lagosuchus talampayensis.
facts.quote: The type specimen of Marasuchus (PVL 3871) had a femur which was 5.75 cm (2.26) inches in length, about 40-50% larger than the type specimen of Lagosuchus talampayensis.

facts.statement: The preserved maxilla of Marasuchus was low with at least 12 teeth, mostly blade-like and serrated, though some rear teeth were leaf-shaped.
facts.quote: The maxilla was low, with at least 12 teeth. Most of these teeth were blade-like and serrated, but some of those near the rear of the bone were less curved and more leaf-shaped.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Marasuchus is a valid genus or a junior synonym of Lagosuchus.
facts.quote: It is sometimes regarded as a junior synonym of Lagosuchus (which would make Marasuchus an invalid later name for Lagosuchus fossils).

facts.statement: A 2019 study suggested that Marasuchus lilloensis might be a synonym of Lagosuchus talampayensis after re-examining the type specimen.
facts.quote: In 2019, the type specimen of Lagosuchus at Universidad Nacional de La Rioja was re-examined by Federico Agnolin and Martin Ezcurra. They noted that the type specimen actually does share several of the diagnostic traits identified by Sereno and Arucci for Marasuchus.

facts.statement: A 2024 study concluded that Marasuchus and Lagosuchus represent the same animal, with Lagosuchus talampayensis having priority.
facts.quote: Otero et al. (2024), in an effort to model the evolution of archosaur biomechanics, also regarded the two species as the same animal, with Lagosuchus talampayensis taking priority.

facts.statement: In 1994, Sereno and Arcucci created the genus Marasuchus for better-preserved fossils because they considered Lagosuchus talampayensis a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: A 1994 study argued that the first species, Lagosuchus talampayensis, has insufficient fossil material to justify its continued use. In response, the same study gave the better-preserved PVL fossils a new genus: Marasuchus.

facts.statement: Marasuchus had dinosaur-like traits in its hip and femur but lacked a perforated acetabulum and had primitive ankle features.
facts.quote: Most of its specific dinosaur-like traits relate to the hip and the head of the femur (thigh bone). Nevertheless, it lacked certain dinosaur-like features such as a perforated acetabulum (open hip socket), and it had several plesiomorphic ("primitive") features of the ankle.

facts.statement: Marasuchus is known from several specimens showing most of its skeleton, but skull material is limited and the hand is entirely unknown.
facts.quote: Marasuchus lilloensis is known from several specimens representing most of the animal's skeletal anatomy, although skull material remains limited and the hand is entirely unknown.

facts.statement: The Marasuchus braincase was tall and typical for early archosaurs but shared some similarities with early dinosaur braincases.
facts.quote: The braincase was tall and fairly typical compared to other early archosaurs. However, in a few cases it shared specific similarities with the braincase of early dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Most of the unique traits that define Marasuchus are found in its vertebrae.
facts.quote: Most of Marasuchus' diagnostic features (i.e. unique or unusual traits which characterize it specifically) occur in its vertebrae.

facts.statement: Marasuchus had a long, curved neck created by elongated neck vertebrae with offset ends, similar to other bird-lineage archosaurs.
facts.quote: Most of the neck vertebrae were elongated and had offset front and rear ends, creating a long and curved neck like that of other avemetatarsalians (bird-lineage archosaurs).

facts.statement: The vertebrae near Marasuchus's hip had expanded, trapezoidal neural spines that touched the spines of adjacent vertebrae.
facts.quote: Vertebrae near the hip were also characteristic to Marasuchus, since their neural spines were also trapezoidal and expanded to such an extent that they contacted those of adjacent vertebrae.

facts.statement: Only two vertebrae attached to the hip in Marasuchus, whereas most dinosaurs typically have three or more.
facts.quote: Two vertebrae attach to the hip, less than in most dinosaurs which typically acquire three or more in the sacrum.

facts.statement: Marasuchus had a characteristically elongated tail where the vertebrae increased drastically in length toward the tip.
facts.quote: The tail was characteristically elongated, with vertebrae drastically increasing in length towards the tip.

facts.statement: Marasuchus's forelimb bones were very slender and shorter than its leg bones, with the entire forelimb being about half the size of the hindlimb.
facts.quote: The forelimb bones (consisting of a humerus, ulna, and radius) were very slender and shorter than the leg bones, and the forelimb as a whole was about half the size of the hindlimb.

facts.statement: No part of Marasuchus's hand has been preserved in the fossil record.
facts.quote: No portion of the hand is preserved.

facts.statement: The upper blade of Marasuchus's hip, the ilium, was similar in general shape to that of Herrerasaurus.
facts.quote: The ilium (upper blade of the hip) was similar to that of Herrerasaurus in general shape.

facts.statement: Marasuchus had an enlarged ischium that was longer than the main portion of its ilium, a trait more developed than in earlier archosauriforms.
facts.quote: However, the ischium was also enlarged relative to earlier archosauriforms, as it was longer than the main portion of the ilium.

facts.statement: Unlike later dinosaurs, Marasuchus retained a bony inner wall in its hip socket (acetabulum) rather than having an open cavity.
facts.quote: However, this had not yet evolved in Marasuchus, which retains a bony inner wall of the acetablum.

facts.statement: Marasuchus had a ridge of bone called the trochanteric shelf that branched from the anterior trochanter and wrapped around the femur shaft.
facts.quote: In addition, Marasuchus also possessed a ridge of bone known as the trochanteric shelf, which branches down from the anterior trochanter and wraps around the shaft of the femur.

facts.statement: In Marasuchus, the tibia (shin bone) was longer than the femur (thigh bone).
facts.quote: The tibia was also longer than the femur.

facts.statement: Marasuchus had five thin, elongated metatarsal foot bones that were close together.
facts.quote: The five metatarsals (foot bones) were thin, elongated, and close together.

facts.statement: Although incomplete, the preserved toe bones suggest Marasuchus had a phalangeal formula of 2-3-4-5-0, similar to other dinosauromorphs.
facts.quote: Although not all of the pedal phalanges (toe bones) were preserved, the phalangeal formula (number of bones per toe) was likely 2-3-4-5-0 as with other dinosauromorphs.

facts.statement: Marasuchus belonged to Avemetatarsalia, the archosaur branch closer to birds and dinosaurs than to crocodilians.
facts.quote: Marasuchus was part of Avemetatarsalia, the branch of archosaurs closer to birds and other dinosaurs rather than to crocodilians.

facts.statement: Marasuchus was classified as a dinosauriform, placing it closer to dinosaurs than to lagerpetids.
facts.quote: More specifically, it was a dinosauriform, meaning that it was closer to dinosaurs than the lagerpetids.

facts.statement: While not as closely related to dinosaurs as silesaurids like Silesaurus, Marasuchus is one of the most completely known avemetatarsalians and helps understand early dinosaur-like evolution.
facts.quote: Although it was not as close as silesaurids such as Silesaurus, Marasuchus is still one of the most completely known avemetatarsalians, assisting knowledge of the early evolution of dinosaur-like characteristics.

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Marasuchus is Marasuchus illoensis.
facts.quote: type_species: Marasuchus illoensis

facts.statement: The species Marasuchus illoensis was described by Sereno and Arcucci in 1994.
facts.quote: type_species_authority: Sereno & Arcucci, 1994

facts.statement: Lagosuchus lilloensis, described by Romer in 1972, is a synonym of Marasuchus.
facts.quote: synonyms: Lagosuchus lilloensis Romer, 1972

facts.statement: Marasuchus was an extinct ornithodiran archosaur that lived during the Middle Triassic (Ladinian, about 230 million years ago) in the Chañares Formation in La Rioja, Argentina.
facts.quote: Marasuchus es un género extinto de ornitodiros, saurópsidos emparentados con los dinosaurios, que vivió a mediados del período Triásico (Ladiniense, hace unos 230 millones de años) en la Formación Chañares situada en La Rioja, Argentina.

facts.statement: Marasuchus was a small predator only 40 centimeters long.
facts.quote: Era un pequeño depredador de solo 40 centímetros de largo.

facts.statement: The species Marasuchus lilloensis was originally described as a second species of Lagosuchus, named L. lilloensis.
facts.quote: La especie Marasuchus lilloensis fue descrita originalmente como una segunda especie de Lagosuchus, L. lilloensis.

facts.statement: In a 1994 restudy, Sereno and Arcucci concluded that the original Lagosuchus type specimen was too poorly preserved to allow adding additional specimens to that genus.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, en un restudio de Lagosuchus realizado por Sereno y Arcucci (1994), los autores concluyeron que el espécimen original (la especie tipo) estaba muy mal preservado como para permitir añadir especímenes adicionales a ese género.

facts.statement: Sereno and Arcucci noted that the L. lilloensis specimen had different limb proportions compared to the type species.
facts.quote: Ellos también notaron que el espécimen de L. lilloensis tenía proporciones diferentes en las extremidades con respecto a la especie tipo.

facts.statement: Based on these differences, Sereno and Arcucci assigned L. lilloensis to the new genus Marasuchus.
facts.quote: Basándose en esto, ellos asignaron a L. lilloensis a un nuevo género, Marasuchus.

facts.statement: Marasuchus lived from 241.464 to 237 million years ago during the Ladinian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Ladinian to Ladinian (241.464 to 237 million years ago)

facts.statement: Marasuchus is one of the most completely known avemetatarsalians, providing key insights into the early evolution of dinosaur-like traits.
facts.quote: Marasuchus is still one of the most completely known avemetatarsalians, assisting knowledge of the early evolution of dinosaur-like characteristics.

rejected.statement: Marasuchus possessed a distinct tab of bone called an anterior trochanter on the outer edge of its femoral head, a feature shared with other dinosauriforms.
rejected.quote: A distinct tab of bone known as an anterior trochanter was present on the outer edge of the femoral head, as with other dinosauriforms.
